ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Geronimo Synthetic CCD

text.paragraph: Establishing care at the clinic for poor sleep, nightmares and drinking at night: a trauma-informed history with the interpreter, PTSD, alcohol, depression and cognitive screening, liver tests, a recent fall, and his safety. Concerns: He wants to sleep through the night without the old battles and the dead coming back to him; He does not want whisky to rule his nights, and he does not want to fall again; He wants care that respects who he is, his people and his own ways of healing. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical biography with true dates. These events are not part of the synthetic care timeline.

tr.td: Eight wounds in wars with Mexican forces, including gunshot wounds of the right thigh (bullet retained), left forearm, left side and back, a saber wound below the right knee, and a glancing shot below the left eye
Blow to the top of the head with a musket butt, with loss of consciousness; no lasting effect recorded
Killing of his mother, wife and three children by Mexican troops, and his grief afterwards in his own words
Prisoner of war since 1886: hard labor at Fort Pickens apart from his family, then Alabama, where many of his people died of disease, and Fort Sill
Twice jailed in the guardhouse for drinking whisky as a prisoner of war, by his own account

list.item: Chiricahua Apache of the Bedonkohe band; an elder respected by his people; lives alone in a small house on the military reservation near Fort Sill, where his people have been held by the federal government since they were brought there; cannot travel or return to his homeland without permission; keeps horses and cattle and works when he wishes [S]

Speaks Chiricahua Apache as his first language, with Spanish and some English; does not read English; chose to have the clinic's Apache-speaking interpreter at every visit; asked to be called Geronimo [S]

Lost his mother, his wife and his three children in an attack by soldiers when he was young; fought for decades; surrendered on promises that were not kept; was held at hard labor apart from his family; and has seen many of his people die in captivity. He spoke of these events briefly and in his own way, and chose what to share [S]

Alcohol: whisky most evenings for the past year, about four to six drinks, more on the nights the memories come; obtained in town; no withdrawal seizures or hallucinations when he has gone without; does not use commercial tobacco (ceremonial use not asked about); no other drugs [S]

Traditional healing: he prays in his own way and has his own ways of healing; he will decide whether and how they are part of his care; the clinic offered access through its traditional medicine program and asked nothing further [S]

Strengths and supports: his standing among his people, his faith, his work with horses and cattle, his skill in telling his own story, a long record of endurance, and clear views about what he wants [S]
No firearm or other weapon in his house; he keeps a knife for work with the cattle [S]

tr.td: Establishing care at the clinic for poor sleep, nightmares and drinking at night: a trauma-informed history with the interpreter, PTSD, alcohol, depression and cognitive screening, liver tests, a recent fall, and his safety
Two-week review, seen the same day by psychiatry: the CAPS-5 interview, the diagnosis, grief, treatment for alcohol use, and the choice of therapy
Six-week review: cognitive processing therapy, naltrexone, sleep, mood and medicine
Eleven-week review: therapy progress, sertraline and sodium, drinking and falls
Sixteen-week review after twelve therapy sessions: symptoms, drinking, safety and his plan
Same-day sick visit for cough and fever

Trauma-informed, culturally safe care: ask how he wishes to be addressed and what matters to him, the Apache interpreter at every visit, time and plain explanations, consent before each question about the past and each examination, no demand to retell the killings or name the dead, and his history shared only as he chooses
Psychiatry consultation at the clinic's visiting session to confirm the diagnosis with a structured interview, weigh grief against prolonged grief disorder, and advise on therapy and medicines
PTSD screening and tracking: PC-PTSD-5 and PCL-5 at intake, a CAPS-5 interview to confirm, and the PCL-5 at each visit

Cognitive processing therapy, twelve weekly sessions with the clinic's behavioral health therapist and the interpreter, without the written trauma account, with worksheets done aloud, shorter sessions when he tires, and video sessions on weeks he cannot come

Medicine for PTSD only if he wants it: sertraline starting at 25 mg with a sodium check within the first month, then 50 mg; no benzodiazepines; prazosin not started now because of his age and recent fall, and reconsidered with standing blood pressure checks if nightmares persist

Alcohol: brief counseling with his own goals, DSM-5-TR criteria, PEth explained as part of care, thiamine, and liver and kidney tests before medicine; no withdrawal medicine needed (no past withdrawal seizures or delirium)
Naltrexone 50 mg daily with liver tests at four to six weeks and at four months, a wallet card about opioid pain medicines, and acamprosate (dose set by kidney function) if naltrexone cannot be used
Safety: a structured safety assessment at intake, a written safety plan in his own words, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, small medicine supplies, and safety review at every visit
Falls: Timed Up and Go at visits, orthostatic blood pressure, no drinking before riding or walking out at night, a light on the path to his house, and an exercise program for strength and balance
Traditional healing offered alongside clinic care at his choice, through the clinic's traditional medicine program, with nothing asked about his beliefs
Vaccines due at his age: pneumococcal conjugate, high-dose influenza, RSV, recombinant zoster and Tdap, at the wellness visit and the following visit
Sleep most nights with nightmares no more than once a week
Nightmares from most nights to about once every two weeks; sleeping six hours most nights
Lower PTSD symptoms by a meaningful amount (PCL-5 down at least 10 to 20 points)
PCL-5 56 to 24 after twelve sessions of cognitive processing therapy
Drink no more than one drink on any day, and no drinking before riding
AUDIT 19 to 5; PEth 236 to 14 ng/mL; one evening of heavy drinking in sixteen weeks
No falls in sixteen weeks; Timed Up and Go 13 to 11 seconds

list.item: Independent in daily activities; rides and walks without a device; Timed Up and Go 13 seconds; one fall in the past month at night after drinking [S]

Alert, oriented, dignified and watchful; speech measured, through the interpreter; mood tired and heavy; affect restricted, warmer when speaking of his horses; startles at a door closing; no psychotic symptoms; no thoughts of suicide or of harming anyone; judgment and insight good [S]

text.paragraph: Structured synthetic safety assessment on 2026-07-08: current ideation absent, intent absent, plan absent. Outpatient care with close follow-up. Risk factors reviewed without detail: post-traumatic stress, moderate alcohol use disorder, depressive symptoms, older age, living alone, a recent fall and many losses. He has no firearm; medicines are dispensed in small amounts. A written safety plan was made with him in his own words through the interpreter, and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988, with interpreter services) and the clinic's number were written on a card he carries. Safety is reviewed at every visit [S]
